ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Thickness Testing | Cincinnati OH
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection on tanks, vessels, piping and steel in Cincinnati, OH. ASNT Level II technicians mobilized. Get a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Cincinnati, Ohio
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Cincinnati plants, river terminals, fabrication shops and steel structures for ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection. We measure remaining wall on tanks, vessels and piping, examine groove welds with angle beams, and write a report your inspector or engineer can act on. Describe the component and the governing code in a quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Cincinnati

The Ohio River gives Cincinnati a long line of barge terminals, and those terminals depend on steel: aboveground storage tanks, loading-arm piping, dock structures and the pressure vessels that sit behind them. Wall loss on tank floors and shells, and on piping that has sat wet for decades, is the classic reason to bring in an ultrasonic technician. Further inland the city's industrial base is mixed. Consumer-products and food plants run steam, compressed air and process piping. Breweries and beverage producers operate jacketed stainless vessels. Machine shops and engine component suppliers make heavy forgings and weldments that are checked for internal quality before they ship.

Bridges and heavy civil work add another category. The Ohio River crossings around the city carry large steel members, and the companion bridge planned beside the Brent Spence Bridge is now moving into construction, with temporary structures and crane equipment arriving by barge. Steel fabrication for projects like that is examined to AWS and state transportation requirements, and ultrasonic examination of groove welds is one of the tools in those codes. Hospitals, universities and commercial towers round out the list with boiler plants and heat exchangers that need periodic thickness checks.

What ultrasonic testing finds, and what it misses

A transducer sends a short sound pulse into the steel and the instrument times the echo. Time converts to distance, so a thickness reading is a direct measurement of remaining wall. In welds, the same physics reveals reflectors inside the volume: lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, slag lines and planar cracks. Laminations in plate and forging flaws also reflect sound.

The method has limits you should hear about before the job. Heavy scale, pitting and rough coating all weaken the signal or scatter it, so surface preparation matters. Very coarse-grained castings and some stainless weld metal attenuate sound and can hide flaws. A crack lying parallel to the sound path may never produce a return. Thin wall near a nozzle or a weld cap geometry can produce echoes that look like flaws and are not. A competent technician identifies these cases and tells you in the report where coverage was limited. Surface-breaking cracks on a weld toe are often better found with magnetic particle inspection in Cincinnati or liquid penetrant testing in Cincinnati.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Cincinnati work

The work is performed to a written procedure that follows the construction or in-service code for the item. For weld examination that usually means ASME Section V Article 4, with acceptance taken from ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 for process piping, or AWS D1.1 for structural steel. Thickness measurement follows ASME Section V Article 23 (SE-797) and ASTM E797, with the owner's inspection program setting where the readings are taken.

For in-service equipment, API 510 covers pressure vessels, API 570 covers piping and API 653 covers aboveground storage tanks. Under those codes the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and reports the data, including thickness at each condition monitoring location, and your inspector uses it for remaining life and interval decisions. Ohio's boiler and pressure vessel law is Chapter 4104 of the Ohio Revised Code, administered through the Division of Industrial Compliance in the Ohio Department of Commerce, so jurisdictional vessels also fall under that regime. Which equipment is covered, who inspects it and how often are questions for the owner's inspection agency. Process plants subject to OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 treat these readings as part of the mechanical integrity record, and our guide to thickness measurement requirements explains the Section V background.

Ultrasonic thickness testing: how a survey is run

On corroded steel the standard tool is a dual-element probe, which has separate transmit and receive crystals and holds up better on pitted or rough surfaces than a single-element probe. The technician calibrates on a step block made of the same material, checks the gauge again at intervals, and displays the A-scan wherever the wall is thin or the surface is pitted, because a bare digital number can double on a thin wall or lock onto a lamination instead of the back wall.

The readings are taken at marked condition monitoring locations so that a future survey measures the same spots. On piping that means a grid at elbows, tees and reducers where erosion concentrates; on tanks it means shell courses and, where accessible, floor and roof plate. Hot lines need a high-temperature probe and couplant, plus a correction for the temperature of the steel. Insulated lines need the insulation opened at the test points, and the owner or a contractor handles that. When a location reads below the minimum thickness the owner's inspector specifies, we tell the owner at once instead of waiting for the report. You can run the numbers yourself with our remaining-life calculator by following the national ultrasonic testing page.

Ultrasonic weld inspection with angle beams

Weld examination uses shear-wave angle beams, typically 45, 60 or 70 degrees, wedged onto the plate on both sides of the weld where access allows. The technician builds a reference level or distance-amplitude curve from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, scans the full weld volume plus the heat-affected zone, and evaluates each indication by amplitude, length and position against the code's acceptance table. Lack of fusion along a bevel face and slag are the typical rejects.

Geometry decides what is practical. Thin plate under a stated thickness limit in some codes is not examined this way. Nozzle-to-shell welds, set-on branches and small-diameter pipe often cannot be scanned from both sides, and the report records the limitation. Where an owner wants to replace film work with ultrasonic examination on a piping or vessel weld, the code must permit it and the engineer and authorized inspector must agree in advance.

Who does the work

Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, approves the company's approach to ultrasonic procedures. Technicians who perform and interpret the examination are Level II under Atlantis's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. An ASNT Level III approves the procedures and reviews reports. Atlantis has no office in Cincinnati, so technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If your own contract or customer requires a particular qualification scheme, name it in your quote request so that we can answer plainly whether it fits.

What the ultrasonic report contains

You receive a document your authorized inspector can place in the equipment file without chasing missing details. The core contents are listed here.

Typical contents of an ultrasonic examination report
ItemWhat is recorded
ComponentEquipment or line number, drawing reference, material, nominal and minimum thickness
ProcedureProcedure number and revision, governing code and edition
EquipmentInstrument, probes, wedges, couplant, calibration block, calibration checks
PersonnelTechnician name and level, Level III reviewer
ResultsThickness grid by location, or weld indications with position, length and amplitude
DispositionAccept or reject against the named criteria, limitations on coverage

Thickness data is delivered as a grid with each location tied to a sketch, which makes trending between campaigns straightforward. Where a reading falls near the minimum, the report shows the value alongside the nominal wall and the calculated loss so that the reviewer sees the trend at a glance, and any location that could not be reached is listed with the reason, such as insulation that stayed in place or a bolted support in the way.

Planning an ultrasonic job in Cincinnati

Cincinnati has real winters and humid summers, and both affect ultrasonic work. Cold steel thickens couplant, and below freezing the technician needs a couplant made for low temperature or has to warm the test area. Wet surfaces after river-valley rain or fog need drying before a weld scan. Summer sun can raise exposed steel to temperatures that call for high-temperature probes. Tell us the season of your outage when you ask for a quote.

Terminal and plant access shapes the schedule more than the weather. Expect safety orientation, hot-work and confined-space permits, and escort rules at river terminals. Scaffolding or rope access to reach tank shells and elevated piping has to be arranged by the owner. Plan for the insulation removal, paint or scale removal and lighting that make a clean reading possible, and tell us where the units sit relative to I-71, I-75 and I-275 so that travel is accounted for. Do not assume how fast a crew can arrive; confirm dates when the scope is agreed.

Ultrasonic, magnetic particle or penetrant testing

Choose ultrasonic testing when you need remaining wall or internal weld quality. Choose magnetic particle testing for surface cracks in carbon steel welds, and penetrant testing for surface cracks in stainless steel, aluminum or nickel alloys. Many Cincinnati jobs use two of them on the same weld. The ultrasonic testing guide explains the method in more depth, and the Ohio inspection services hub lists the state's other service pages.

Training your own ultrasonic technicians in Cincinnati

If you would rather build in-house capability, Atlantis trains technicians through UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with simulator practice on the ultrasonic testing simulator. Hands-on practice and the practical exam take place at the employer's facility, and the employer certifies personnel under its written practice. See our Cincinnati NDT training page for the route.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Cincinnati?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Cincinnati. Qualified technicians are mobilized to your plant, terminal or fabrication shop for the agreed scope, and we confirm dates when the job is defined instead of promising an arrival time in advance.

faq.q: What can ultrasonic testing measure on a Cincinnati storage tank or vessel?
faq.a: It measures remaining wall thickness at marked condition monitoring locations and can show laminations and internal weld flaws. It does not replace a visual or surface crack examination, which are separate methods chosen by the inspector.

faq.q: Who decides whether a vessel or piping system is fit for service?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector or engineer makes that decision under API 510, API 570 or API 653. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and reports thickness and weld data in a form the inspector can use.

faq.q: Which codes do you apply to ultrasonic weld inspection?
faq.a: The procedure follows ASME Section V Article 4 and takes acceptance criteria from the construction code, such as ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12, ASME B31.3 or AWS D1.1. You name the governing code and edition when you request a quote.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my Cincinnati welds?
faq.a: Only where the construction code allows it and the owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree before the job. Some codes permit ultrasonic examination of production welds, and others require film or digital images. Ask before you plan the scope.

faq.q: How should surfaces be prepared before a thickness survey?
faq.a: Remove loose scale, flaking paint and insulation at the test points, and leave a clean metal or firmly bonded coating surface. Heavy corrosion products or rough weld spatter reduce signal quality and may need grinding before readings are reliable.

faq.q: Do cold or hot Cincinnati conditions affect ultrasonic readings?
faq.a: Yes. Cold stiffens ordinary couplant and hot steel needs high-temperature probes, couplant and a temperature correction. Tell us the expected surface temperatures so the technician arrives with the right materials for the season.

faq.q: What happens if a reading is below minimum thickness?
faq.a: The technician tells your site contact when the reading is confirmed and records it in the report. Your authorized inspector then decides on repair, rerating, re-inspection interval or removal from service, because those are owner decisions.

faq.q: Can my own staff learn ultrasonic testing instead of hiring a crew?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and Level 2 training with simulator practice. The employer provides hands-on practice and the practical exam under its written practice, and the employer certifies its own technicians.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Cincinnati, OH | MT
mt.description: Mag particle testing for welds, castings and structural steel in Cincinnati, OH. Wet fluorescent and visible methods, ASNT Level II technicians. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Cincinnati, Ohio
mt.html:
Magnetic particle inspection finds surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, and Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to Cincinnati for that work: weld toes on steel structures, pressure equipment welds, crane and lifting components, castings and forgings. We use yokes, prods and wet fluorescent or visible methods to suit the part, and we report each indication against the code you name. Send the part, the code and the location through a quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where mag particle testing is used in Cincinnati

Cincinnati makes and moves a great deal of steel. Fabrication shops weld frames, platforms, tanks and skids that are examined before they ship. Machine builders and engine component suppliers produce forgings, shafts and gears that need a check for cracks before assembly. Railroads and river terminals run cranes, hoists, chains and hooks whose fatigue-prone details are examined on a schedule. Distribution centers and plants have runway beams and lifting lugs that come under similar scrutiny.

Heavy civil work adds to the demand. Steel bridge girders and cross frames over the Ohio River carry cyclic loads, and welds at stiffener and gusset connections are classic locations for fatigue cracking. The companion bridge now moving into construction beside the Brent Spence Bridge shows how large steel projects here are supported by temporary structures and heavy lifts, all of which rely on welded attachments and lifting hardware. Process plants and terminals also have pressure vessels, tank shell-to-nozzle welds and piping supports where surface cracks are looked for in carbon steel.

What the method finds, and what it misses

A magnetic field is induced in the part. Where a crack interrupts the field at or near the surface, flux leaks out and attracts fine iron particles, which outline the crack. That is why the method is so fast on welds and machined surfaces. It detects surface-breaking discontinuities and slightly subsurface ones, but only in ferromagnetic material: carbon steel and most low-alloy steels. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys do not respond, and penetrant testing is used instead.

Direction matters. A crack lies undetected if it runs parallel to the field, so the part is examined twice with the field at roughly right angles. Thick paint, heavy scale and weld spatter hold the particles away from the surface and can mask a tight crack, so the surface needs cleaning. A buried flaw deeper than a few millimeters will not be found. For internal quality or remaining wall, ultrasonic testing in Cincinnati is the better tool.

Codes and acceptance criteria used for Cincinnati steel

The procedure follows ASME Section V Article 7 and ASTM E1444, with ASTM E709 as the guide to the method. Acceptance comes from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel, and AWS D1.5 for bridge steel inspected for the state transportation department. For in-service equipment under API 510, API 570 and API 653, the owner's authorized inspector remains the inspector of record, and Atlantis supplies the crack indications and sketches.

Ohio regulates boilers and pressure vessels under Chapter 4104 of the Ohio Revised Code, administered through the Division of Industrial Compliance in the Ohio Department of Commerce. If the vessel is jurisdictional, the owner's inspection agency decides how repair welds are examined. Our explanation of Article 7 requirements covers the technical rules in more detail, and the complete guide to magnetic particle testing gives the general background.

How a magnetic particle examination is carried out

Most field work uses an electromagnetic yoke. An AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, which the technician verifies with a test weight before work begins. On heavy sections where a yoke cannot induce enough field, prods or a coil are used under a procedure that sets current for the thickness.

Particles come in two forms. Dry powder is common on rough weld surfaces outdoors, while wet suspension applied from an aerosol or bath gives higher sensitivity. Fluorescent particles are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area, and the lighting limits are set in the Article. A field indicator or a pie gauge shows that the field is strong enough and is in the right direction. Each area is examined in two directions at roughly right angles. After the examination, demagnetization is done where residual magnetism would disturb later welding, machining, instruments or bearing surfaces.

Weld toes, lifting hardware and fatigue-critical details

Most cracks that matter on Cincinnati steel start at stress concentrations: the toe of a fillet weld, the end of a cover plate, a sharp reentrant corner, the root of a thread. Cranes, hooks, shackles, spreader beams and runway hardware see repeated load, and a crack that begins as a hairline at a weld toe can grow across a section over many cycles. Magnetic particle examination is the quickest way to look at those areas because it works through thin coatings and needs no couplant or darkroom.

For lifting devices, the examination is usually specified by the owner's inspection program or by the lifting standard in force at the site, and the acceptance criteria are often stricter than a general fabrication code, with no linear indications allowed at all. Tell us which standard the owner follows so the report can be written against the right rule, and ask your lifting-equipment engineer whether paint removal is acceptable on the load-bearing parts.

Surface preparation and the cold-weather problem

A clean surface decides the quality of the examination. The technician removes loose scale and oil, and the owner arranges grinding or blasting where coating or spatter is heavy. Thin non-magnetic coatings are acceptable when the procedure has been demonstrated through them, but the allowed thickness is limited and has to be shown.

Cincinnati winters make wet methods harder. Particle suspensions stiffen in the cold, and ice on steel prevents contrast. A part that is cold and wet can also break the continuity of the particle film. The procedure sets the temperature range for materials, and the technician warms the area or uses a dry method when the weather requires it.

Judging indications and avoiding false calls

Not every particle buildup is a crack. Magnetic writing from contact with another magnet, sharp changes in section, the edge of a weld cap and the boundary between weld and base metal can all collect particles. A trained technician learns to separate relevant indications from non-relevant ones, and the procedure explains how to resolve a doubtful call: demagnetize, clean, reexamine with a different field direction, or dress the surface lightly and look again.

Each relevant indication is measured, and its length and shape are checked against the acceptance table in the code. In many codes rounded and linear indications are judged differently, and the length-to-width ratio decides which rule applies. Cracks and lack of fusion are rejected whatever their size. The technician marks each rejectable area on the part, photographs it where the owner wants a record, and tells the site contact before leaving so repair planning can begin early. If the owner prefers, the repair weld and the final examination can be scheduled as a follow-up visit once the grinding is finished, which avoids leaving an open question in the equipment file.

Who performs the examination

Level II technicians perform and interpret the inspection under Atlantis's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. Atlantis has no office in Cincinnati, so technicians are mobilized to the site for the scope you define. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, and the technician arrives with calibrated equipment and the approved procedure.

What the magnetic particle report contains

The report identifies the component and its drawing, names the procedure revision and code edition, and lists the yoke or other equipment with its lifting-power check, the particles and lighting used, and the technician and Level III reviewer. Each indication is recorded with its location, orientation and length, then dispositioned as acceptable or rejectable against the named criteria. Sketches or photographs of marked locations are attached. If an area could not be examined because of access or coating, the report says so plainly. The lifting-power check of the yoke and the field-strength check on the part are written down as well, so a reviewer months later can see that the examination was set up correctly and not simply assumed to be.

Photographs are optional but useful. A picture of a marked indication beside a scale, taken before grinding, is often the only evidence that survives once a repair has been made, and it helps the owner's engineer decide whether similar welds elsewhere should be examined as well.

Planning a magnetic particle job in Cincinnati

River-valley humidity and cold mornings affect both surface condition and particle behavior, so give us the season and whether the work is indoors or exposed. Arrange lighting for fluorescent work and a shaded or enclosed space where daylight would wash out the indications. Terminals and plants require orientation and permits, and elevated welds on tanks, bridges or racks need scaffolding or lift access that the owner supplies. Confirm the grinding scope for weld caps and toes, because the technician cannot examine what is not accessible.

Tell us how far the site is from the I-71, I-74 and I-75 corridors so travel is planned properly, and expect dates to be confirmed when the scope is set instead of at the time of the enquiry.

Magnetic particle, penetrant or ultrasonic testing

Pick magnetic particle testing for surface cracks in carbon steel. Pick penetrant testing when the material is stainless, aluminum or any non-magnetic alloy, or when the part cannot be magnetized. Add ultrasonic testing when the weld volume or remaining wall also matters. For other services in the state see the Ohio inspection services hub, and for the national overview read about magnetic particle testing services.

Training your own magnetic particle technicians

Atlantis teaches MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, with the practical exam and hands-on work at your facility under your written practice. Start with the Cincinnati NDT training page or check the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker.

faq.q: What materials can magnetic particle testing inspect in Cincinnati?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic materials, which means carbon steel and most low-alloy steel. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys do not respond to magnetic flux, so liquid penetrant testing is used on those materials instead.

faq.q: Does magnetic particle testing find cracks below the surface?
faq.a: It finds surface-breaking cracks and flaws just beneath the surface, generally within a few millimeters. Deeper internal flaws need ultrasonic testing, so the method should not be treated as a volumetric inspection of a weld.

faq.q: Why is the part examined in two directions?
faq.a: A crack running parallel to the magnetic field produces little flux leakage and may not show. ASME Section V Article 7 requires two examinations with the field at roughly right angles so cracks in any direction are found.

faq.q: Is fluorescent or visible particle testing used in the field?
faq.a: Both are used. Visible particles work in daylight on rough welds, while fluorescent particles give higher sensitivity but need UV-A light and a darkened area. The choice is set by the procedure, the surface and the code.

faq.q: Do you demagnetize parts after examination?
faq.a: Yes, when residual magnetism could interfere with welding, machining, instruments or bearing surfaces. The procedure sets out when demagnetization is needed, and the report notes that it was carried out and measured afterward.

faq.q: What surface preparation does a Cincinnati weld need before mag particle testing?
faq.a: Remove loose scale, oil and spatter so the particles can reach the metal. Thin firmly bonded coatings may be acceptable if the procedure has been demonstrated through them, but thick paint usually has to come off.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle testing be done in cold Ohio weather?
faq.a: Yes, with changes. Ice and cold suspensions reduce contrast, so the area is warmed or a dry method is selected. The procedure sets the allowed temperature range, and the technician records the conditions in the report.

faq.q: Who decides whether an indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The technician evaluates indications against the acceptance criteria in the governing code and records the result. For in-service equipment, the owner's authorized inspector makes the final fitness-for-service decision using that data.

faq.q: Can my team learn magnetic particle testing instead of outsourcing it?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and Level 2 training. The employer arranges hands-on practice and the practical exam under its written practice and certifies its own technicians under SNT-TC-1A.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye PT Inspection | Cincinnati
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection for stainless, aluminum, nickel alloy and steel welds and castings in Cincinnati, OH. ASNT Level II technicians. Get a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Cincinnati, Ohio
pt.html:
Liquid penetrant testing, often called dye penetrant inspection, finds cracks and porosity that break the surface of any non-porous material. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to Cincinnati for penetrant work on stainless steel vessels and piping, aluminum and nickel alloy parts, castings, machined components and weld repairs. We follow the procedure your code requires and report every indication. Use a quote request to describe the material and surface, and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Cincinnati

Penetrant testing is the practical choice wherever a material cannot be magnetized, and Cincinnati has plenty of it. Breweries, beverage producers and food plants have stainless tanks, jacketed vessels, sanitary piping and heat exchangers, where welds are examined after fabrication or repair. Chemical and consumer-products plants use stainless and nickel alloy piping, and pharmaceutical-style processes demand clean, smooth weld surfaces that penetrant inspection can check without damage.

The region's engine and machinery supply chain also generates penetrant work. Machine shops finish aluminum, titanium and nickel alloy parts, castings need a check for surface porosity and shrinkage cracks, and weld repairs on cast components are examined at the end of each repair cycle. The aerospace cluster around Cincinnati and the large number of suppliers behind it mean many parts are examined to the customer's drawing and specification, so we ask for that document at the start. Power plants and terminals along the Ohio River also have alloy piping and valve bodies where penetrant testing supports repair decisions.

What the method finds and what it misses

A low-viscosity liquid is drawn by capillary action into discontinuities that are open to the surface. After excess penetrant is removed, a developer pulls the trapped liquid back out and shows the crack as a visible line or dot. The method finds surface-breaking cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts and porosity on ferrous and non-ferrous metals, ceramics and some plastics.

It cannot find anything that does not reach the surface. A crack closed by smeared metal from grinding, machining, shot peening or abrasive blasting will not accept penetrant, which is why surface condition and sometimes etching matter. Porous materials soak up penetrant and give a false background. Oil, paint, rust and chemical residues block entry, so cleaning is the most important step. When a weld also needs internal examination, use ultrasonic testing in Cincinnati, and when it is carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection is often quicker.

Codes and acceptance criteria for penetrant work

The procedure follows ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165, with ASTM E1417 used where a specification calls for it. Acceptance criteria come from the governing code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 for structural steel where penetrant testing is specified. Under API 510, API 570 and API 653 the owner's authorized inspector remains the inspector of record, and Atlantis supplies the examination data.

Ohio's boiler and pressure vessel law, Chapter 4104 of the Ohio Revised Code, is administered through the Division of Industrial Compliance in the Ohio Department of Commerce. Where a jurisdictional vessel is repaired, the owner's inspection agency decides how the repair welds are examined, and penetrant testing is a common answer for stainless and alloy repairs. Our article on Section V Article 6 gives the detailed rules.

Penetrant types and methods

Penetrants are classified by whether they are visible or fluorescent and by how they are removed. Visible, solvent-removable penetrant in aerosol cans is the field workhorse for welds on vessels and piping, because it needs no darkened area or special lighting. Fluorescent penetrants give higher sensitivity and are examined under UV-A light in a dark space, which suits shop work and critical parts. Water-washable and post-emulsifiable systems are used in a shop setting for production parts and castings.

Material compatibility is not a detail. Penetrant materials used on nickel alloys and austenitic stainless steel must be controlled for sulfur and halogen content so they do not harm the metal in service. The procedure states the limits, and the technician records the batch of materials used.

Compatibility also covers the equipment itself. Some elastomers, plastics and coatings on or near the part can swell or stain when exposed to solvents, so the technician masks or avoids them. Parts that will see oxygen service, hydrogen service or very high temperature may carry cleanliness requirements that exclude certain developers altogether, and the owner's engineer should tell us about those before the kit is chosen.

How the examination is performed

The technician cleans the surface and lets it dry, applies penetrant by spray, brush or dip, and holds it for the dwell time set by the procedure. Excess is removed, developer is applied in a thin even coat, and the area is examined after the development time and again as indications grow. Light levels are checked for visible work, and UV-A intensity and ambient light are checked for fluorescent work.

Temperature is a hard limit. The standard range under ASME Section V Article 6 is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for both the part and the penetrant materials. Outside it, the procedure has to be qualified for the actual temperature. Cincinnati winter mornings fall below that range often, and sun-heated stainless in July can exceed it, so the technician measures surface temperature before starting and the report records it.

Reading indications and weld repairs

Penetrant indications fall into two groups. Relevant ones come from real discontinuities, such as a crack that shows as a sharp line or a row of pores that shows as a string of dots. Non-relevant ones come from surface conditions: a rough weld ripple, a scratch, a machining mark or a leftover bit of penetrant in a crevice. The procedure allows the technician to wipe the spot, reapply developer and look again to settle a doubtful call.

Weld repairs follow a fixed order. After a defect is ground out, the cavity is examined to prove the crack is gone, the repair weld is made, and the finished weld is examined again. Skipping the first step is a common cause of repeated failure, so we recommend agreeing the sequence with your welding engineer before work begins. Final examination is usually performed after any required heat treatment or pressure test, because those steps can open cracks that were not visible before.

For cast components the same logic applies to machining. A casting that shows clean after rough machining can reveal shrinkage porosity once more metal is removed, so many owners ask for a second examination at the finished dimension. State in the quote request whether the part is raw, rough machined or finished so the technician plans the surface condition and the developer choice correctly. Thin or highly polished sanitary surfaces need a light touch with the developer so that the film does not hide small indications or leave a deposit that must later be removed.

Cleaning before and after

Cleaning is half the job. Solvents, detergents and mechanical methods remove oil, grease, paint and scale, and the part must dry fully before penetrant is applied, since trapped solvent dilutes the penetrant and weakens indications. After the examination the developer and any penetrant residue are removed, which matters for stainless vessels in food and beverage service, for parts that will be welded, and for components entering oxygen or other cleanliness-controlled service. Agree who supplies the cleaning materials, how waste rags and solvents are handled on the site, and what rinse or final-cleanliness requirement your quality team applies.

Who performs the work

Level II technicians perform and interpret penetrant examinations under Atlantis's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports. Atlantis has no office in Cincinnati, so technicians are mobilized to your site for the scope you define. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

What the penetrant report contains

You receive a report with the component, material, drawing and weld numbers, the procedure revision and governing code edition, and the penetrant, remover and developer brand and batch. It records surface temperature, dwell and development times, the technician and Level III reviewer, and each indication with its location, size and type. Every indication is accepted or rejected against the named criteria, with photographs or sketches where useful and a note on any area that could not be examined.

Planning a penetrant job in Cincinnati

Tell us the material, the finish and the weld condition. Ground and blasted surfaces may need etching to reopen cracks, and the owner has to approve etching on finished parts. Stainless equipment in food and beverage plants must be left free of residues, so agree cleaning and rinse procedures with your quality team before work. Cold and humid conditions in the Ohio River valley can slow drying and prevent the area from reaching the temperature range, so state the season and whether the work is indoors. On exposed work, a tent, a portable heater or a shaded work window can be the difference between a valid examination and a postponed one, and the owner usually has to arrange them.

Disposal and housekeeping matter on an operating plant. Aerosol cans, solvent-soaked rags and developer residue are handled under the site's waste rules, and the technician leaves the work area clean so the next trade is not delayed by leftover film on the steel.

Plants require safety orientation and often hot-work or confined-space permits. Tell us how the site connects to I-71, I-74, I-75 and I-275 so travel is planned. Dates are confirmed when the scope is set, and we do not promise an arrival time at the enquiry stage.

Penetrant, magnetic particle or ultrasonic testing

Use penetrant testing for stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and any other non-porous metal, and for parts that cannot be magnetized. Use magnetic particle testing on carbon steel when speed matters, and ultrasonic testing when internal quality or remaining wall is the question. The MT versus PT comparison helps choose between the two surface methods, the national penetrant testing page describes the service, and the Ohio inspection services hub links the rest of the state.

Training your own penetrant technicians

Atlantis teaches PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, and technicians can rehearse the method on the penetrant testing simulator. Hands-on work and the practical exam happen at the employer's facility, and the employer certifies its own people. Start from the Cincinnati NDT training page.

faq.q: What materials can liquid penetrant testing inspect?
faq.a: Any non-porous material, including carbon steel, stainless steel, aluminum, titanium and nickel alloys, as well as ceramics and some plastics. It is the standard choice where magnetic particle testing cannot be used.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find internal flaws in a weld?
faq.a: No. It finds only discontinuities that are open to the surface. For internal weld quality or remaining wall thickness, ultrasonic testing is the appropriate method, and many jobs combine the two.

faq.q: What temperature range applies to penetrant testing in Cincinnati?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 sets 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature, so winter and summer conditions need planning.

faq.q: Why does surface preparation matter so much?
faq.a: Penetrant has to enter the crack. Oil, paint, rust and smeared metal from grinding or blasting can seal the opening, so the surface must be cleaned and sometimes etched before the examination to avoid missing real cracks.

faq.q: Is visible or fluorescent penetrant used in the field?
faq.a: Visible solvent-removable penetrant is common in the field because it needs no darkened area. Fluorescent systems give higher sensitivity and are used where UV-A light and a dark space are available, often in shops.

faq.q: Can penetrant materials harm stainless steel or nickel alloys?
faq.a: They can if sulfur or halogen content is not controlled. The procedure sets limits for these materials, the technician uses controlled products, and the report records the brand and batch used.

faq.q: How does penetrant testing compare with magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Magnetic particle testing is faster on carbon steel but only works on ferromagnetic material. Penetrant testing works on almost any non-porous metal but depends heavily on surface cleanliness, so the choice follows the material.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects the indications found?
faq.a: The technician evaluates each indication against the acceptance criteria in the governing code. For in-service equipment, the owner's authorized inspector or engineer decides on repair or continued service using that data.

faq.q: Can I train my own staff in penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 and Level 2 training with simulator practice. The employer provides hands-on practice and the practical exam under its written practice and certifies its own technicians.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing (RT) Alternatives | Cincinnati, OH
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States. For Cincinnati, OH we offer UT as a volumetric alternative and Level III review of RT work.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Cincinnati, Ohio: What Atlantis Offers
rt.html:
Atlantis does not perform radiography anywhere in the United States. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity regulated by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission under 10 CFR Part 34, or by the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and it is not a service Atlantis offers here. If you searched for radiographic testing in Cincinnati, this page explains what we can do that is useful to you.

Ultrasonic testing as a volumetric alternative

Where the construction code and the owner allow it, ultrasonic examination can take the place of film or image work for volumetric examination of welds. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 gives its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII allows ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only under specific conditions. None of that is automatic. The substitution must be agreed with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job starts.

Atlantis mobilizes qualified technicians to Cincinnati sites for this work. Our ultrasonic testing page for Cincinnati explains the technique, and the national ultrasonic testing page describes the service. You can also read our ultrasonic testing guide.

Level III review of radiographic work

Many Cincinnati owners receive film or digital images from a licensed contractor and need a second opinion. An ASNT Level III can review existing images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. That includes a second read on a disputed indication, a check that the technique sheet and image quality indicators match the requirement, and a review of a contractor's procedure and written practice. This is a desk-based review of records and images and needs no radiation licence. The review is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis does not recommend or name radiography contractors, and the owner remains responsible for choosing one.

The same service is available through our Level III consulting service, and we can help you structure written practice development if your program has gaps.

Radiographic testing theory and training

Technicians who need to understand radiographic technique can study the theory through our radiographic testing Level 2 course. The course covers principles, exposure geometry, image quality and code interpretation. Practical radiography requires a licensed employer and a qualified radiation safety program, and that part sits with the employer. Employers certify personnel under their own written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and see the Cincinnati NDT training page for the training route.

What to send with an enquiry

A short package makes the conversation quicker. Send the drawing or isometric, weld numbers, the governing code and edition, the material and thickness, and the contract clause that calls for volumetric examination. Say whether the owner has already agreed to ultrasonic examination in place of film or image work, and who will accept the results. With that, the scope, procedure and Level III review can be set out clearly.

Other conventional methods in Cincinnati

Surface and thickness methods are available at the same site visit. See magnetic particle inspection in Cincinnati for carbon steel welds and liquid penetrant testing in Cincinnati for stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys. For a state overview, visit the Ohio inspection services hub. To discuss a Cincinnati scope, send a quote request and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in Cincinnati?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under 10 CFR Part 34 or the equivalent Agreement State rules and is not a service we offer here.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my welds?
faq.a: Sometimes. The construction code must permit it, and the owner, engineer and authorized inspector must agree before the job. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 each have their own provisions that need to be checked.

faq.q: What does a Level III review of radiographic images involve?
faq.a: An ASNT Level III reviews existing film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, and can give a second read on disputed indications without any radiation licence.

faq.q: Can you recommend a radiography contractor in Cincinnati?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not recommend or name radiography contractors. We can review a contractor's procedure, written practice and images once you have chosen one, and give you an independent technical opinion.

faq.q: Where can technicians study radiographic theory?
faq.a: A radiographic testing Level 2 theory course is available from Atlantis. Practical exposure work needs a licensed employer and radiation safety program, so the employer arranges that part and certifies its own personnel.
